beside.text: But it didn't reach everything. A lot of the child stuff around my attachment to women was still there. When I later tried [self-directed inner-child therapy](https://youtu.be/yEWFjODXJbI?si=IXUqrhExojOm6Itm), it felt like I was making it up at first. That didn't stop me from practicing, but I did stop when I felt fake, stop in the sense of ... like I might still kind of allow the exercise to play out somehow but I would stop "pushing" it to be a certain way, and I'd stop trying to feel it was realer than it was. I would go more into listening and waiting mode rather than imagining mode.

rows.start: Years later, I found a warm, intuitive inner child therapist

beside.label: Before
beside.text: I found the therapist, Daja, years later, randomly, and gave it a shot, although I didn't think I needed it. But she did actually help me see some things more clearly. For example, she had me write down how many people I could fully trust as a child (lots), then how many people I could fully trust as an adult (zero). That was difficult, and it's actually the opposite of what you might expect from inner-child therapy, since usually that's about people who had problems trusting as a child.

rows.label: Your last paragraph before the map, without "in general and map it out completely" (one of the "too verbatim" ones)
rows.start: It also showed me that I really do need to count more on mys

beside.label: Before
beside.text: It also showed me that I really do need to count more on myself than I assumed. I need to be much better as an inner adult for my inner child, because my childhood was actually so nice that I kind of just assume I can trust everyone, and that gets me into trouble. So it got me curious to learn more about inner-child therapy in general and map it out completely, which is a process I'm still in the midst of as I test this guide with people.

headings: # Building Trust With Your Little One
## Not Every Hero Wears A Cape

rows.label: Your Not Every Hero P2 (103.2)
rows.start: You can protect your little one from yourself too, like by r

beside.label: Before
beside.text: You can protect your little one from yourself too, like by repairing after an internal attack. "What's an 'internal attack'?" Calling yourself an idiot for losing your keys again, for one. Your little one was listening, so you go back and apologize to them. If they're sarcastic about it, you hear it out instead of snapping back. They don't trust you yet, and you don't ask them to. They complain about something, and if they're right, you say so. All of that shows as clearly to them as the clean room did. It's evidence you're safe to be around and that you accept them. Love needs both, but without warmth they can still feel like they're only being put up with.

headings: # When the Adult Voice Feels Fake

rows.start: How many tries would I give it? It's not like we can just pu

beside.label: Before
beside.text: How many tries would I give it? It's not like we can just put a number on it. Some things shift in a day. Others take about as long as learning guitar. But do notice if it progress is stagnating. If it’s making things worse, or you just can’t do it right now, I’d change course sooner (stopping counts).
